challenges.name: ports-for-payment-and-email-quiz
challenges.title: Is OrderService really behind a port?
challenges.description: Two pieces of code from the OrderService refactor: a test that uses fakes passed through the constructor, and a PaymentGateway interface copied from the payment SDK.

questions.explanation: True. OrderService receives its payment gateway, mailer and repository through the constructor and only knows the port interfaces, so the test decides what the gateway answers: here a decline, with no HTTP call at all. Nothing in the code under test opens a connection, so a CI job without network can run it, and the declined path is as easy to reach as the happy path. Before the refactor, placeOrder created HttpPaymentClient itself, so every test talked to the sandbox and a decline needed the provider's magic card numbers. The misconception is that you need the real provider (or its sandbox) to test payment logic: you need it to test the adapter, not the rules in OrderService.

False. The interface is a copy of one vendor's API: its request and result types come from @acme-pay/sdk, and OrderService branches on that vendor's outcome strings. A provider that answers state and transactionRef cannot implement createCharge(ChargeRequest): VendorCharge without pretending to be Acme, so either the adapter fakes Acme's types or OrderService and its tests change. A port is useful when it is written in the application's words (charge(orderId, learnerId, amountVnd) returning succeeded/declined) and owned by the code that uses it; translating to a vendor is the adapter's job. The misconception is that any interface decouples you; an interface shaped like the vendor keeps the coupling and only adds a layer.

challenges.name: order-service-ports
challenges.title: Put payment and email behind ports in OrderService
challenges.description: OrderService.placeOrder sells a premium CodeDev course. Today it creates HttpPaymentClient and SmtpEmailClient inside placeOrder, so it only works with the network and no test can make a card decline or the mail server fail. Refactor it so that the class is built as new OrderService({ payments, emails, orders }), where payments is a PaymentGateway, emails an EmailSender and orders an OrderRepository (the three port interfaces are given in the starter and must not change), and placeOrder uses only these ports. Keep the behaviour exactly as specified above placeOrder: an invalid price (not a positive whole number) gives invalid_price and an existing paid order gives already_owned, both without charging; otherwise take an id from orders.nextId() and call payments.charge(orderId, learnerId, priceVnd); if charge throws, return payment_unavailable and save nothing; a declined charge saves the order as payment_failed with chargeId null, sends no email and returns payment_declined with the reason; a successful charge saves the order as paid with the charge id, then calls emails.sendReceipt(email, orderId, courseTitle, priceVnd) and returns receiptSent true, or receiptSent false when sending throws. The test runner reads { paidBefore?, payments?, emails?, checkouts } from stdin, builds OrderService with recording fakes, places each checkout and prints the result with every port call, then a summary line (summary only for more than 10 checkouts). Wiring the real clients through adapters is not graded.
hints: If OrderService may not call new HttpPaymentClient, where does it get something it can call charge on, and who decides whether that something is the real provider or a fake?

Look at the OrderServiceDeps type and at the two places in placeOrder that create a vendor client. The port methods take different arguments and return different shapes than the vendor methods, so the code around those two calls changes too, not only the line with new.

A similar refactor on a different service: a ProgressService that did `const clock = new SystemClock(); const now = clock.currentTimeMillis();` becomes `constructor(private readonly deps: { clock: Clock })` with `interface Clock { now(): Date }`, and the method reads `this.deps.clock.now()`. A test then passes `{ now: () => new Date("2026-10-26T00:00:00Z") }` and the behaviour is the same as before, only the source of the time moved.

tests.name: A paid checkout: charge, save as paid, send the receipt
tests.expected:
placeOrder u_an nodejs-api-security -> paid ord_1, receipt sent
  charge ord_1 u_an 249000 -> succeeded
  save ord_1 u_an nodejs-api-security 249000 paid ch_1
  sendReceipt an@codedev.test ord_1 "Authentication & Session Design" 249000 -> ok
summary: 1 charges, 1 paid orders, 0 failed orders, 1 receipts

tests.name: A declined card is saved as payment_failed and gets no receipt
tests.expected:
placeOrder u_an nodejs-api-security -> payment_declined (card_declined)
  charge ord_1 u_an 249000 -> declined:card_declined
  save ord_1 u_an nodejs-api-security 249000 payment_failed -
placeOrder u_binh nodejs-ai-engineering -> paid ord_2, receipt sent
  charge ord_2 u_binh 149000 -> succeeded
  save ord_2 u_binh nodejs-ai-engineering 149000 paid ch_2
  sendReceipt binh@codedev.test ord_2 "Building LLM Features with TypeScript" 149000 -> ok
summary: 2 charges, 1 paid orders, 1 failed orders, 1 receipts
